SEC-HD-V8-01.note: Two axes at once: head noun 'shipment' is singular (kills A,B) and 'since the war' forces perfect aspect (kills C). Long relative clause with plural 'blades' as the attractor. Good item.

SEC-HD-V8-02.note: Matched-pair punctuation: the supplement opens with a comma after 'east range', so it must close with a comma, not a dash. Number ('range' singular) kills C,D. Dash options are only eliminable if the reader looks back at the opening comma, which is the right kind of work.

SEC-HD-V8-03.note: D is defensible. 'who' is right in both B and D (subject of 'had falsified'; 'the others believed' is parenthetical), so the item reduces to restrictive vs nonrestrictive, which is a semantic/contextual judgement, not a convention. I chose B because four partners exist and the clause identifies which one, but a reader who takes 'the partner' as already fixed by 'whichever partner happened to be in the city' can punctuate it as a supplement and be defended by Chicago 6.27. Also note A and C are eliminable from the option text alone (whom + finite verb), so the set halves without the passage.

SEC-HD-V8-04.note: Dangling participle: 'Having lost the count' needs a human subject, killing A and C; present perfect in D clashes with 1898 and with 'the expedition came home'. Two independent axes, cleanly done.

SEC-HD-V8-05.note: Correlative parallelism: 'not only the number of stoppages but also the tedium'. B fails the correlative pair on option text alone (and also), so one distractor is eliminable blind - borderline weak.

SEC-HD-V8-06.note: C is defensible. 'More than one' is conventionally singular, but 'more than one OF the twelve tenants' is exactly the construction where notional/proximity agreement with the plural of-phrase is recognised in edited usage (CGEL, and Garner's exceptions for a following plural). Since past reference already kills A and D, a student who reads the of-phrase as head has a principled route to 'were turned away'. This is the item I would most expect a defensible-second dispute on.

SEC-HD-V8-07.note: TWO problems. (1) C and D are eliminable with the passage covered: a comma before a restrictive 'that' is never right, so the set halves blind. (2) The completed sentence looks like a fragment on every option: 'The surveyors' notebooks that still survive in the same archive, and they record...' leaves the subject with no main verb, because 'survive' is consumed by the relative clause. Worth an author's second look independent of the key.

SEC-HD-V8-08.note: Linking verb takes a predicate adjective ('smells sweet', not 'sweetly') and 'A cellar' is singular. But the same sentence later contains 'the same cellar three weeks later ... smells of nothing anybody would praise' - a parallel that hands over both the number and the verb form. Not within four words of the blank, so I left the flag false, but it is a giveaway.

SEC-HD-V8-09.note: 'each of' is singular (kills A) and the resurveying precedes the 1861 request, so past perfect. D ('was already resurveyed') is the near-miss; 'already ... at least twice' before a stated past point wants the perfect, so I do not think D is defensible, but it is the closest call in the batch after 03.

SEC-HD-V8-10.note: Gerund-phrase subject ('reconciling the entries...') is singular; 'In the years the wharf was in use' is a closed past frame, killing the perfect options.

SEC-HD-V8-11.note: 'as well as' does not compound the subject; 'when the bandmaster retired' is a fixed past point, so simple past. Same shape as 12 and 14.

SEC-HD-V8-12.note: 'The tracings ... along with the pattern books' is plural; 'were losing' is eliminable on option text alone (nonsensical active progressive with no object), so at least one distractor falls blind. Easiest of the agreement items.

SEC-HD-V8-13.note: Three-part infinitive series; only C is an infinitive, so the answer is visible from the option shapes once you know one earlier element is 'to sample'. B is eliminable blind (a finite clause in a series of phrases).

SEC-HD-V8-14.note: C is defensible. Tense is settled ('were sold' -> 'was'), so it turns entirely on the possessive's antecedent, which is genuinely ambiguous: 'their' points at 'the two presses' (grammatical head of the subject), but 'its' can point at 'a mission' - the sentence's only other salient owner and the natural owner of 'remaining type' after a sale - and the opening line's 'a hand press ... without ITS type' primes exactly that. The item asks the student to pick an antecedent the text does not disambiguate.

SEC-HD-V8-15.note: The interrupter 'in the same wallet as the awards themselves' opened with a comma after 'contains' and must close with one before the object 'a list'; no comma may separate 'a list' from its 'of' phrase. All four options are shape-identical, so nothing falls blind. One of the better items here.

SEC-HD-V8-16.note: Same mechanism as 15: the appositive 'a volume rebound so often that...' must close with a comma before the main verb 'records'. A colon would not close a supplement and D double-punctuates. Note the appositive semantically describes the minute book, not 'the list' that governs the verb - grammatically legal but a little untidy.

SEC-HD-V8-17.note: BROKEN AS WRITTEN. Three options join the clauses legally. D (semicolon + comma) is the fullest form, but a comma after a sentence-initial conjunctive adverb is optional in edited American English (Chicago 6.57: 'usually followed by a comma'), which makes both C ('; consequently the series') and B ('. Consequently the series') defensible. Only A is clearly wrong (comma splice). This item cannot distinguish D from C on any convention I can name.

SEC-HD-V8-18.note: 'not only X but also Y' agrees with the nearer element ('the village schoolmaster'), and 'In the decade after the first policies were sold' closes the past frame. Clean.

SEC-HD-V8-19.note: 'The remains' is plural, killing B and D. A vs C is then tense only: the present is fixed by 'twice the length of what IS left' at the end of the sentence. Slightly unusual for the number axis not to finish the job.

SEC-HD-V8-20.note: 'The clauses' is plural across a long modifier chain ending in the singular 'width'; 'for sixty years' from 1751 is closed, and the coordinate clause 'no two counties copied' is past, so simple past passive.

SEC-HD-V8-21.note: Past counterfactual: the 'would have collapsed' apodosis fixes 'had reached'. A ('would have' in the if-clause) is eliminable blind by anyone who knows the rule. Would be a giveaway on the hard route.

SEC-HD-V8-22.note: Introductory 'Because' clause takes a closing comma; 'the yard had fitted' is a restrictive relative and must not be fenced. All four options are shape-matched 2x2, nothing falls blind.

SEC-HD-V8-23.note: Sequence of tenses in reported speech after 'reported in 1889', plus 'exhaust' used intransitively in B and D, which is eliminable without the passage. Two axes but both cheap.

SEC-HD-V8-24.note: 'one of the very few works ... that credit' - the relative modifies the plural 'works'. C and D are eliminable with the passage covered (comma before restrictive 'that'), so the set halves blind, exactly as in 07. The singular 'credits' is the classic attraction-to-'one' error; widespread in speech but not in edited prose, so I did not flag it as defensible.

rules.rule: In every subject-verb item, discard any option using perfect aspect ('has been'/'have been'/'has gone'/'have gone'). The key is the simple past or simple present.
rules.fired: 8 of 9 (06, 09, 10, 11, 12, 18, 19, 20); fails only on 01, where the key IS the present perfect
rules.why_it_matters: Nine items are built as a 2x2 of {singular, plural} x {simple, perfect}. Aspect is decidable from the time adverbial almost mechanically, and once a solver notices that the perfect is nearly always the trap, each of these items collapses to a coin-flip on number before any reading of the subject. I was applying this by item 12 and it kept paying. Item 01 is the only inoculation, and one exception in nine is not enough to break the habit.

rules.rule: In punctuation items offering an option with a comma before 'that', that option is always wrong.
rules.fired: 07 and 24, both times, and both times it removed two of the four options with the passage covered

rules.rule: Where a supplement/interrupter is opened earlier in the sentence, the key is the option that closes it with a single matched comma and adds nothing else.

cross_item_heuristic.answer_letter_pattern: My 24 picks come out exactly 6 A / 6 B / 6 C / 6 D. If the key matches, the spread is uniform to the item - which is good hygiene, but flat-uniform is itself a pattern: a solver who is confident on 18 items can allocate the remaining 6 by counting letters. Worth checking whether the spread is uniform per quarter as well as overall, since the previously shipped permutation tell in this repo also read as a perfect histogram.
cross_item_heuristic.no_pattern_found_in: There is no length, hedging, or comma-count tell that I could detect. Key length rank looked random.

template_groups.shared: One template, nine times: a long noun phrase whose head disagrees in number with an adjacent attractor, and a 2x2 option set crossing number with aspect. Solving two teaches the rest. This is 38% of the batch on a single frame; a real module 2 would not repeat it this often.

Sub-template of the above with an explicit non-compounding phrase ('as well as' / 'along with' / 'together with') fenced by commas. 14 swaps the verb for a possessive pronoun but the reasoning is identical.
Quantifier subject ('more than one of the twelve tenants' / 'each of the four pits') followed by a plural of-phrase and a relative clause.

Identical mechanism and identical option geometry: a supplement must be closed with a comma immediately before the element that completes the main clause, with a punctuation-heavy decoy. Solving one gives the other outright.
2x2 of a second issue crossed with 'comma before restrictive that'. The comma axis is free in both, so both are effectively two-option items.
Matched-pair supplement punctuation crossed with a second axis (number, who/whom, restrictiveness).
Both hang on 'not only ... but also', 05 for parallelism and 18 for agreement. Not solvable from each other, but a student primed by one will spot the other instantly.
